summary:
The challenge of Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions is to create a way for astronauts to self-monitor their own health in an easy-to-read way. Early on in our research, we discovered NASA's own 5 hazards of space travel. What stood out is that while the rest could be measured, isolation and confinement would be trickier. So, taking advantage of the option for "gamification," we decided to design our application around Tomogachi or Virtual Pets. By improving the health of your pet, you improve your own health as well. 
We monitor the users' vitals to ensure they are within correct levels and indicate via a coloring system how well the astronaut is doing, and it is reflected in the pet. Some of the difficulties that must be faced in this regard are the fact that some of the data that is gathered must be input manually and some of the data can be monitored. Additionally, while we had fun, some metrics are essential and do take away from the “game”.  
	With this system, we can have astronauts monitoring their health levels in a fun and informative yet simple and quick-to-notice way. What we strive for is efficiency in relaying the data.
details:
What it Does & How it Works:

 It is first and foremost a dashboard with several components to showcase the vitals of the astronaut. You have the main screen, which has key vitals, such as BPM, hydration levels, and the cabin climate. It also has a wheel that switches between body vitals, cabin data, our logs, and the lab samples, and next to it a list of tasks that one should do to maintain their health. And the star of the main is the Virtual Pet Avatar, a squid creature that will indicate its state based on the data that is monitored and manually inputted and will showcase different states based on how the health of the astronaut is going. 

Switching from the main panel to the spacewalk panel shows the vitals of the astronaut when they are outside, for instance, on the ISS. We see in this one how long we've been outside, the core temperature of the astronaut, Helmet C02, the suit oxygen level, etc. 

At last, we have the history panel that showcases all the data that we saved and the trends throughout the past 2 weeks. The main areas of vitals would be the Sleep & Mood, Heart & Lungs, Fuel & Body, Brain & Eyes, and finally, Cabin data. This is a long laundry list of information that will be important for the astronaut to know about. 

Something else that should be mentioned would be the debug menu, which showcases, at least for the moment, how different levels of data would look in the system. An example of this would be lowering our heart rate to its lowest levels, which would have a flashing indicator that something is wrong, and the Virtual Pet Avatar would begin to indicate that it isn’t feeling well. The debug menu is a nice way to showcase how these different changes would change the layout and virtual pet avatar on the device dashboard. 

 Benefits & intended impact: 

Its benefit is information and having access to it. What we intend with this is for this to be readily available to the astronaut as an individual. When it comes to monitoring health, especially with these space missions, it is easy to focus on the whole. To worry about the crew as a unit rather than how the individual is doing. Especially for the individual astronauts themselves. So having access to one’s own information and having them keep track of information that needs to be manually inputted. Along with reminders from our own system, allows for one to remind themselves of their health as more than just for the mission. But for their own sake!

Tool and Technologies Used:

For this project, we used a plethora of technology. We will be upfront about our use of LLMs to help us with designing and building our projects. We used agents like Claude, ChatGPT as tools. But we also used the Node platform for the project. 

What Makes It Creative: There is a lot of the project that is purely the fundamentals for the idea of software that monitors the health of an astronaut. Keeping track of monitored health data and manually inputting data are key components of any software of this nature. And the addition of externalities such as cabin climate and radiation dose. However, what makes it creative is how it interacts with the Virtual Pet Avatar. Having a fun and easy indicator for the health of the astronaut allows for a simpler and more efficient way of communicating health status to an astronaut. Especially if the Virtual Pet has status changes and makes comments to indicate what the astronaut needs to work on. 

How We Used The Data: 

We used the NASA Data, a wide array of data from all available resources, to create synthetic data that would be used to showcase how it would look on the dashboard. So we want to have our base data based on the already existing data that NASA gave us, while also allowing for you to change how the data is shown via the debug menu.
